entries.name: ClassicalMechanics.eulerLagrangeOp
entries.docstring:
The Euler Lagrange operator, for a trajectory `q : Time → X`,
  and a lagrangian `Time → X → X → ℝ`, the Euler-Lagrange operator is
    `∂L/∂q - dₜ(∂L/∂(dₜ q))`.
entries.snippet: noncomputable def eulerLagrangeOp (L : Time → X → X → ℝ) (q : Time → X) : Time → X

entries.name: ClassicalMechanics.eulerLagrangeOp_eq
entries.snippet:
lemma eulerLagrangeOp_eq (L : Time → X → X → ℝ) (q : Time → X) :
    eulerLagrangeOp L q = fun t => gradient (L t · (∂ₜ q t)) (q t)
    - ∂ₜ (fun t' => gradient (L t' (q t') ·) (∂ₜ q t')) t

entries.name: ClassicalMechanics.eulerLagrangeOp_zero
entries.snippet:
lemma eulerLagrangeOp_zero (q : Time → X) :
    eulerLagrangeOp (fun _ _ _ => 0) q = fun _ => 0

entries.name: ClassicalMechanics.euler_lagrange_varGradient
entries.snippet:
theorem euler_lagrange_varGradient
    (L : Time → X → X → ℝ) (q : Time → X)
    (hq : ContDiff ℝ ∞ q) (hL : ContDiff ℝ ∞ ↿L) :
    (δ (q':=q), ∫ t, L t (q' t) (fderiv ℝ q' t 1)) = eulerLagrangeOp L q

entries.name: ClassicalMechanics.hamiltonEqOp
entries.docstring:
Given a hamiltonian `H : Time → X → X → ℝ` the operator which when
  set to zero implies the Hamilton equations.
entries.snippet:
noncomputable def hamiltonEqOp (H : Time → X → X → ℝ) (p : Time → X) (q : Time → X) :
    Time → X × X

entries.name: ClassicalMechanics.hamiltonEqOp_eq
entries.snippet:
lemma hamiltonEqOp_eq (H : Time → X → X → ℝ) (p : Time → X) (q : Time → X) :
    hamiltonEqOp H p q = fun t => (∂ₜ q t + -gradient (fun x => H t x (q t)) (p t),
      - ∂ₜ p t + -gradient (fun x => H t (p t) x) (q t))

entries.name: ClassicalMechanics.hamiltonEqOp_eq_zero_iff_hamiltons_equations
entries.snippet:
lemma hamiltonEqOp_eq_zero_iff_hamiltons_equations (H : Time → X → X → ℝ)
    (p : Time → X) (q : Time → X) :
    hamiltonEqOp H p q = 0 ↔
    (∀ t, ∂ₜ q t = gradient (fun x => H t x (q t)) (p t)) ∧
    (∀ t, ∂ₜ p t = -gradient (fun x => H t (p t) x) (q t))

entries.name: ClassicalMechanics.hamiltons_equations_varGradient
entries.snippet:
theorem hamiltons_equations_varGradient
    (H : Time → X → X → ℝ) (pq : Time → X × X) (hp : ContDiff ℝ ∞ pq)
    (hL : ContDiff ℝ ∞ ↿H) :
    (δ (pq':= pq), ∫ t, ⟪(pq' t).1, ∂ₜ (Prod.snd ∘ pq') t⟫_ℝ - H t (pq' t).1 (pq' t).2) =
    fun t => hamiltonEqOp H (fun t => (pq t).1) (fun t => (pq t).2) t

entries.name: Electromagnetism.OneDimPointParticle.gaussLaw

entries.name: Electromagnetism.OneDimPointParticle.gaussLaw_iff
entries.docstring:
For the charge distribution of a point particle in 1-dimension, a static electric field
  satifies Gauss's law if and only if it is the linear combination of the
  electric field `electricField q ε` (corresponding to the symmetric step function), plus
  a constant electric field.

  The `if` direction of this result is easy to prove, whilst the `only if` direction
  is difficult.

  Note: This result follows from the (as yet unproven) analgous result for the
  vacuum.
entries.snippet:
@[sorryful]
lemma gaussLaw_iff (q ε : ℝ) (E : StaticElectricField 1) :
    E.GaussLaw ε (chargeDistribution q) ↔ ∃ m, E = electricField q ε + constD 1 m

entries.name: Electromagnetism.OneDimVacuum.gaussLaw_iff
entries.docstring:
An electric field obey's Gauss's law for the vacuum in 1 dimension if and only if

entries.snippet:
@[sorryful]
lemma gaussLaw_iff (q ε : ℝ) (E : StaticElectricField 1) :
    E.GaussLaw ε (chargeDistribution) ↔ ∃ m, E = constD 1 m

lemma divergence_eq_sum_fderiv {s : Finset E} (b : Basis s 𝕜 E) {f : E → E} :

entries.name: divergence_prodMk
entries.snippet:
lemma divergence_prodMk [FiniteDimensional 𝕜 E] [FiniteDimensional 𝕜 F]
    {f : E×F → E} {g : E×F → F} {xy : E×F}
    (hf : DifferentiableAt 𝕜 f xy) (hg : DifferentiableAt 𝕜 g xy) :
    divergence 𝕜 (fun xy : E×F => (f xy, g xy)) xy
    =
    divergence 𝕜 (fun x' => f (x',xy.2)) xy.1
    +
    divergence 𝕜 (fun y' => g (xy.1,y')) xy.2

entries.name: divergence_add
entries.snippet:
lemma divergence_add {f g : E → E} {x : E}
    (hf : DifferentiableAt 𝕜 f x) (hg : DifferentiableAt 𝕜 g x) :
    divergence 𝕜 (fun x => f x + g x) x
    =
    divergence 𝕜 f x + divergence 𝕜 g x

entries.name: divergence_neg
entries.snippet:
lemma divergence_neg {f : E → E} {x : E} :
    divergence 𝕜 (fun x => -f x) x
    =
    -divergence 𝕜 f x

entries.name: divergence_sub
entries.snippet:
lemma divergence_sub {f g : E → E} {x : E}
    (hf : DifferentiableAt 𝕜 f x) (hg : DifferentiableAt 𝕜 g x) :
    divergence 𝕜 (fun x => f x - g x) x
    =
    divergence 𝕜 f x - divergence 𝕜 g x

entries.name: divergence_const_smul
entries.snippet:
lemma divergence_const_smul {f : E → E} {x : E} {c : 𝕜}
    (hf : DifferentiableAt 𝕜 f x) :
    divergence 𝕜 (fun x => c • f x) x
    =
    c * divergence 𝕜 f x

entries.name: divergence_smul
entries.snippet:
@[sorryful]
lemma divergence_smul [InnerProductSpace' 𝕜 E] {f : E → 𝕜} {g : E → E} {x : E}
    (hf : DifferentiableAt 𝕜 f x) (hg : DifferentiableAt 𝕜 g x)
    [FiniteDimensional 𝕜 E] :
    divergence 𝕜 (fun x => f x • g x) x
    = f x * divergence 𝕜 g x + ⟪adjFDeriv 𝕜 f x 1, g x⟫

entries.name: Distribution
entries.docstring:
An `F`-valued distribution on `E` (where `E` is a normed vector space over `ℝ` and `F` is a
normed vector space over `𝕜`) is a continuous linear map `𝓢(E, 𝕜) →L[𝕜] F` where `𝒮(E, 𝕜)` is
the Schwartz space of smooth functions `E → 𝕜` with rapidly decreasing iterated derivatives. This
is notated as `E →d[𝕜] F`.

This should be seen as a generalisation of functions `E → F`.
entries.snippet:
abbrev Distribution (𝕜 E F : Type) [RCLike 𝕜] [NormedAddCommGroup E] [NormedAddCommGroup F]
    [NormedSpace ℝ E] [NormedSpace 𝕜 F] : Type

entries.name: Distribution.ofLinear
entries.docstring:
The construction of a distribution from the following data:
1. We take a finite set `s` of pairs `(k, n) ∈ ℕ × ℕ` that will be explained later.
2. We take a linear map `u` that evaluates the given Schwartz function `η`. At this stage we don't
  need `u` to be continuous.
3. Recall that a Schwartz function `η` satisfies a bound
  `‖x‖ᵏ * ‖(dⁿ/dxⁿ) η‖ < Mₙₖ` where `Mₙₖ : ℝ` only depends on `(k, n) : ℕ × ℕ`.
4. This step is where `s` is used: for each test function `η`, the norm `‖u η‖` is required to be
  bounded by `C * (‖x‖ᵏ * ‖(dⁿ/dxⁿ) η‖)` for some `x : ℝ` and for some `(k, n) ∈ s`, where
  `C ≥ 0` is a global scalar.

entries.name: Distribution.diracDelta
entries.docstring:
Dirac delta distribution `diracDelta 𝕜 a : E →d[𝕜] 𝕜` takes in a test function `η : 𝓢(E, 𝕜)`
and outputs `η a`. Intuitively this is an infinite density at a single point `a`.
entries.snippet: def diracDelta (a : E) : E →d[𝕜] 𝕜

entries.name: Distribution.diracDelta'
entries.docstring:
Dirac delta in a given direction `v : F`. `diracDelta' 𝕜 a v` takesn in a test function
`η : 𝓢(E, 𝕜)` and outputs `η a • v`. Intuitively this is an infinitely intense vector field
at a single point `a` pointing at the direction `v`.
entries.snippet: def diracDelta' (a : E) (v : F) : E →d[𝕜] F

entries.name: Distribution.derivative
entries.docstring:
Definition of derivative of distribution: Let `u` be a distribution. Then its derivative is
`u'` where given a test function `η`, `u' η := -u(η')`. This agrees with the distribution generated
by the derivative of a differentiable function (with suitable conditions) (to be defined later),
because of integral by parts (where the boundary conditions are `0` by the test functions being
rapidly decreasing).
entries.snippet: def derivative : (ℝ →d[𝕜] 𝕜) →ₗ[𝕜] (ℝ →d[𝕜] 𝕜) where

entries.name: Distribution.fderivD
entries.docstring:
The Fréchet derivative of a distribution.

Informally, for a distribution `u : E →d[𝕜] F`,
the Fréchet derivative `fderiv u x v` corresponds to the dervative of `u` at the
point `x` in the direction `v`. For example, if `F = ℝ³`
then `fderiv u x v` is a vector in `ℝ³` corrsponding to
`(v₁ ∂u₁/∂x₁ + v₂ ∂u₁/∂x₂ + v₃ ∂u₁/∂x₃, v₁ ∂u₂/∂x₁ + v₂ ∂u₂/∂x₂ + v₃ ∂u₂/∂x₃,...)`.

Formally, for a distribution `u : E →d[𝕜] F`, this is actually defined
the distribution which takes test function `η : E → 𝕜` to
`- u (SchwartzMap.evalCLM v (SchwartzMap.fderivCLM 𝕜 η))`.

Note that, unlike for functions, the Fréchet derivative of a distribution always exists.

entries.name: LorentzGroup.genBoostAux₂_basis_minkowskiProduct

    ⟪genBoostAux₁ u v (Vector.basis μ), genBoostAux₂ u v (Vector.basis ν)⟫ₘ =

    (LinearMap.toMatrix Vector.basis Vector.basis (genBoostAux₂ u v)) μ ν =
      η ν ν * (- (u.1 μ + v.1 μ) * (u.1 ν + v.1 ν)
      / (1 + ⟪u.1, v.1⟫ₘ))

entries.name: LorentzGroup.genBoostAux₁_add_genBoostAux₂_minkowskiProduct
entries.snippet:
lemma genBoostAux₁_add_genBoostAux₂_minkowskiProduct (u v : Velocity d) (μ ν : Fin 1 ⊕ Fin d) :
    ⟪genBoostAux₁ u v (Vector.basis μ) + genBoostAux₂ u v (Vector.basis μ),
    genBoostAux₁ u v (Vector.basis ν) + genBoostAux₂ u v (Vector.basis ν)⟫ₘ =
    2 * η μ μ * η ν ν * (- u.1 μ * (u.1 ν + v.1 ν)
      - u.1 ν * (u.1 μ + v.1 μ)
      + (u.1 μ + v.1 μ) * (u.1 ν + v.1 ν) * (1 + ⟪u, v.1⟫ₘ)⁻¹ +
      2 * u.1 μ * u.1 ν)

entries.name: LorentzGroup.basis_minkowskiProduct_genBoostAux₁_add_genBoostAux₂

entries.name: LorentzGroup.generalizedBoost_timeComponent_eq
entries.docstring:
The time component of a generalised boost is equal to
```
1 +
    ‖u.1.timeComponent • v.1.spatialPart - v.1.timeComponent • u.1.spatialPart‖ / (1 + ⟪u.1, v.1⟫ₘ)
```

A proof of this result can be found at the below link:
https://leanprover.zulipchat.com/#narrow/channel/479953-PhysLean/topic/Lorentz.20group/near/523249684

Note that the decleration of this semiformal result will be similar once
the TODO item `FXQ45` is completed.
entries.snippet:
@[sorryful]
lemma generalizedBoost_timeComponent_eq (u v : Velocity d) :
    (generalizedBoost u v).1 (Sum.inl 0) (Sum.inl 0) = 1 +
    ‖u.1.timeComponent • v.1.spatialPart -
      v.1.timeComponent • u.1.spatialPart‖ / (1 + ⟪u.1, v.1⟫ₘ)
